extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners and parties participating in PTAB inter partes review proceedings (petitioners and patent owners), especially those handling design-patent IPRs
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and procedural guidance the PTAB applies when deciding whether to institute an inter partes review of a design patent, including burdens on petitioners, how to evaluate obviousness under LKQ (Graham factors adapted to design patents), and evidentiary requirements for prior-art (printed publication) web references.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institution standard under 35 U.S.C. § 314(a)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pursuant to 35 U.S.C. § 314(a), the Director may not authorize an inter partes review unless the information in the petition and preliminary response “shows that there is a reasonable likelihood that the petitioner would prevail with respect to at least 1 of the claims challenged in the petition.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The petition must present evidence and argument sufficient to demonstrate a reasonable likelihood of prevailing on at least one challenged claim. Even where the petition meets this standard, institution remains discretionary — the Board may still deny institution for other reasons (see Discretionary Denial rubric).

rubrics_metrics.name: Petition particularity requirement (burden from onset)
rubrics_metrics.description: “In an [inter partes review], the petitioner has the burden from the onset to show with particularity why the patent it challenges is unpatentable.” (citing Harmonic Inc. v. Avid Tech., Inc.; 35 U.S.C. § 312(a)(3); 37 C.F.R. § 42.104(b)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A petition must identify with particularity the evidence supporting each ground and where each claim element is found in the cited patents/printed publications. This particularity requirement is described as 'of the utmost importance.' Failure to identify grounds/evidence with particularity can be a basis to deny institution. Provide clear citations, explicit mapping of elements, and direct evidentiary support (e.g., attested captures for web pages).

rubrics_metrics.name: Board discretion to deny institution
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board is never compelled to institute review; institution remains discretionary even when a petitioner demonstrates a reasonable likelihood of prevailing (citing Harmonic Inc., Adaptics Limited v. Perfect Co., and PTAB practice guidance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of bases for discretionary denial include petitions that unduly burden the patent owner or the Board (e.g., excessive/unclear grounds), failure to satisfy procedural requirements, or other equities. If a petition collapses many distinct challenges into few headings without adequate particularity, the Board may consider denial on discretionary grounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design-patent obviousness standard post-LKQ (apply Graham factors)
rubrics_metrics.description: Following LKQ Corp. v. GM Global Tech. Operations LLC (en banc), obviousness of a design patent is determined using factual criteria similar to those for utility patents under § 103 — application of the Graham factors adapted for designs: (1) scope and content of the prior art (identify a primary reference), (2) differences between claimed design and prior art (visual comparison from perspective of an ordinary designer), (3) level of ordinary skill in the art (ordinary designer), and (4) objective evidence (secondary considerations) when in evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply each Graham factor explicitly in the design context: identify the primary reference (closest/most visually similar), compare overall visual appearance from an ordinary designer's perspective (not isolated features), resolve the ordinary designer skill level, and address any secondary considerations (commercial success, praise, copying) if present. Cite the 2024 Updated Guidance and LKQ for methodology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary reference identification and nature
rubrics_metrics.description: A primary reference must be identified and is generally the closest prior art most visually similar to the claimed design, though it need not be 'basically the same.' The primary reference will typically be in the same field of endeavor but need not be, so long as it is analogous art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The primary reference must be an actual, existing reference ('something in existence') rather than an assemblage of isolated features from various references. Do not treat a collage of features as a single primary reference. Explain why the chosen primary reference is the appropriate starting point and how it is analogous/related.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overall visual appearance comparison (avoid feature cherry-picking)
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare the visual appearance of the claimed design with prior art 'from the perspective of an ordinary designer in the field of the article of manufacture.' Do not compare only selected features; consider the overall visual impression of the designs as a whole (citing In re Harvey and LKQ).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not selectively choose discrete features to the exclusion of other features that materially affect overall impression (dimensions, corner radii, positions, counts of elements, presence/absence of closures/mounts, etc.). Demonstrate how the overall impression of the prior art is visually similar to the claimed design. Explicitly address differences and explain why they would not change the overall impression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Designer of ordinary skill in the art (design context)
rubrics_metrics.description: For design patents, the person of ordinary skill is treated as 'the designer of ordinary capability who designs articles of the type presented in the application.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When defining the ordinary designer, specify education/experience parameters relevant to the field (the decision adopted an uncontested proposal: a bachelor’s degree in industrial design or equivalent, or two years' experience designing cameras or camera housings). Use this persona when assessing what would be known, findable, or predictable to that designer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim construction standard in IPRs and design-specific guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims in an IPR proceeding are construed 'using the same claim construction standard that would be used to construe the claim in a civil action under 35 U.S.C. [§] 282(b).' (37 C.F.R. § 42.100(b)). For design patents, tribunals should not treat claim construction as requiring a detailed verbal description; 'a design is better represented by an illustration.' (Egyptian Goddess).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rely primarily on the drawings for design claim scope. A verbal description is not required but can be helpful to point out particular features relative to the prior art; if provided, ensure it accurately captures the overall visual impression rather than creating a narrow hindsight-focused description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Printed-publication/public-accessibility standard for web references
rubrics_metrics.description: Under 35 U.S.C. § 311(b), IPR petitions may only rely on patents or printed publications. The petitioner bears the burden to identify with particularity evidence sufficient to establish a reasonable likelihood that a reference was publicly accessible before the critical date; whether something is a 'printed publication' is a case-by-case factual inquiry into accessibility (citing Acceleration Bay, In re Lister, Samsung Elecs. v. Infobridge).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide concrete evidence that an ordinary designer could have reasonably found the specific webpage before the critical date (e.g., reliable archived captures, attestation showing the specific URL/page). Indexing is not required, but some evidence of discoverability is critical. Be mindful that discrepancies between an asserted exhibit and an attested archive (differences in content, quality, presence of later-date comments or links) can undermine public-accessibility claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to explain combination/modification (motivation to combine)
rubrics_metrics.description: When asserting obviousness based on combinations of references, the petitioner must sufficiently explain why and how a designer of ordinary skill would combine the references and make the proposed modifications to reach the claimed design.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not merely assert that features from multiple references could be combined; provide reasoned motivation and explanation for the combination and show that the combined/modified result would give the same overall visual appearance as the claimed design. Explain why the modifications are within the ordinary designer's routine skill and do not require impermissible hindsight reconstruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of annotated figures and selective highlighting
rubrics_metrics.description: Annotated figures that selectively highlight discrete features (colored boxes, callouts) are not necessarily adequate to show visual similarity of designs and may be unhelpful if they ignore overall appearance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid relying solely on annotated comparisons that isolate features; use side-by-side overall comparisons and address overall impression and all material differences. If annotated figures are used, ensure they do not obscure differences in shape, proportion, corner radius, and relative positions that affect the overall visual impression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity/numbering of grounds and undue burden on patent owner
rubrics_metrics.description: A petition should clearly enumerate each distinct ground; collapsing numerous distinct challenges into a small number of headings without clarity makes meaningful response difficult and can unduly burden the patent owner and the Board.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If multiple distinct combinations or alternative grounds are asserted, explicitly list and analyze each. Explain why each ground is necessary and avoid presenting ambiguous or overlapping combinations. The Board may consider the number and clarity of grounds in discretionary institution decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secondary considerations (Graham factor four) — objective evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Secondary considerations (when in evidence) are objective indicia of nonobviousness, such as commercial success, industry praise, and copying.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Address secondary considerations where the record contains relevant evidence. If none are presented, state that the record lacks such arguments (as in this decision). When present, tie the evidence (sales, awards, direct evidence of copying) to the claimed design and explain whether it supports nonobviousness.
